program.title: Pricing Strategy Profitability and Commercial Execution
program.subtitle: A ten week self study syllabus for pricing analysts
program.intro: This program develops the ability to recommend a price, quantify its expected financial return, and turn the recommendation into a workable commercial plan. The syllabus combines economics, profitability analysis, customer value, sales execution, and measurement.
program.tools: Excel or Google Sheets required. SQL and Python optional.
program.final_output: An end to end pricing recommendation with financial case and commercial launch plan
how_to_use: Choose one product, service, or anonymized business case and reuse it throughout the program.
Keep a research log. Record each source, its claim, the evidence used, and how the finding affects a pricing decision.
Finish the weekly output before moving on. The outputs become sections of the capstone recommendation.
Use revenue and profit separately. A price that maximizes revenue may not maximize contribution or operating profit.
learning_outcomes: Build a price and margin waterfall from list price to pocket margin.
Calculate contribution, break even volume, price volume tradeoffs, and initiative ROI.
Estimate and interpret own price, cross price, and promotional elasticity.
Use customer value and willingness to pay research to set price ranges.
Design tiers, bundles, fences, discount rules, and commercial guardrails.
Evaluate competitive responses and distinguish useful market evidence from price matching.
Plan a price change with sales enablement, customer communication, governance, and performance tracking.
Present a recommendation that links evidence to revenue, margin, customer impact, and execution risk.

weekly_rhythm.what: Read or watch the core material and write a one page summary in your own words.
Find two additional sources and test whether they agree on assumptions and limitations.
Build the weekly model or analysis using a small dataset.
Translate the analysis into a recommendation for sales, finance, product, or leadership.
Complete the self check and note what still needs clarification.

study_setup: Create one workbook with tabs for assumptions, transactions, economics, elasticity, scenarios, and the final profit bridge.
Use an anonymized company case, public data, or a realistic simulated dataset. Keep the same case for all ten weeks.
Create a folder for weekly outputs and name each file with the week, subject, and version date.
Schedule one challenge session in week 10 with a colleague, mentor, or study partner who can question the assumptions.
program.completion_standard: The program is complete when the capstone recommendation is internally consistent, uses evidence appropriate to the decision, reconciles to a financial return, and includes a commercial plan that another team could execute. A certificate is optional. The durable proof of learning is the model, research log, and decision quality shown in the capstone.

weeks.title: Pricing economics and the profit model
weeks.outcome: Build a baseline model that connects a price decision to volume, revenue, contribution, operating profit, and return on investment.
weeks.summary: Price is usually the most powerful profit lever, but only if you know which profit measure you're optimising and how much volume you can afford to lose. This week gives you the arithmetic every later week depends on: margin vs markup, contribution, break-even volume change, relevant costs and the price waterfall.

concepts.title: Five different profit measures
concepts.syllabus_text: Revenue, gross profit, contribution margin, operating profit, and cash are different measures and answer different questions.
concepts.one_liner: Name the measure you're optimising - revenue, gross profit, contribution, operating profit and cash can disagree.
concepts.explainer: Revenue is what customers pay. Gross profit subtracts cost of goods sold. Contribution subtracts every cost that moves with volume (including variable selling, servicing and payment costs), so it shows what one more sale adds towards fixed costs. Operating profit also subtracts fixed operating costs. Cash is about timing: a profitable sale on 90-day terms still drains cash today. A pricing recommendation should say which of these it maximises, because they can point in different directions.
concepts.example: A price cut can raise revenue while lowering contribution, if the extra customers are expensive to serve or the lost margin per unit outweighs the extra units.
concepts.lending_lens: For a merchant cash advance (MCA), fee income is the revenue line, but the real economics come after partner/broker commission, cost of funds and expected credit loss. Cash timing depends on how fast the holdback repays the advance.

concepts.title: Margin vs markup
concepts.syllabus_text: Margin percentage uses price as the denominator. Markup percentage uses cost as the denominator.
concepts.one_liner: Same profit, different denominator: margin divides by price, markup by cost.
concepts.explainer: If price is 100 and cost is 60, profit is 40. Margin = 40/100 = 40%. Markup = 40/60 = 66.7%. Mixing them up is one of the most common pricing errors: someone told to 'add a 40% margin' who adds 40% to cost (price 84) actually earns a 28.6% margin. Convert with markup = margin / (1 - margin) and margin = markup / (1 + markup).
concepts.example: Cost 60, target 40% margin: price = 60 / (1 - 0.40) = 100. Cost 60 plus a 40% markup: price = 84, margin 28.6%.

concepts.title: Price changes work through unit economics AND volume
concepts.syllabus_text: A price change affects profit through both unit economics and the customer volume response.
concepts.one_liner: A price move changes profit per unit and the number of units - you need both to judge it.
concepts.explainer: Raising price increases contribution per unit but usually loses some customers. The key question is how much volume you can lose before total contribution falls. With contribution margin CM% and a price change dP (both as fractions of the old price), the break-even volume change is -dP / (CM% + dP). Because the price change lands entirely on contribution, low-margin businesses are very sensitive to price, and price cuts need far more extra volume than price increases can afford to lose.
concepts.example: Contribution margin 40%. A 5% increase breaks even if you lose up to 11.1% of volume (0.05/0.45). A 5% cut needs 14.3% more volume (0.05/0.35) just to stand still.

concepts.title: Relevant costs
concepts.syllabus_text: Relevant costs are the costs that change because of the decision. Fully allocated cost can still matter for reporting and long run viability.
concepts.one_liner: Only costs that change because of the decision belong in the decision.
concepts.explainer: For a pricing decision, include costs that move with it: materials, transaction costs, servicing, commissions, and any fixed costs that genuinely change (new staff, new systems). Sunk costs and overheads that stay the same whatever you decide are irrelevant to the short-run choice. But allocated cost still matters over the long run: if every product is priced only above variable cost, nothing pays for the building, the tech team or management, and the business shrinks.
concepts.example: Accepting a one-off order with spare capacity: the relevant cost is the extra materials and labour, not a share of factory depreciation.
concepts.lending_lens: Per deal, cost of funds, expected loss and commission are relevant. Head-office overhead is not relevant to one deal's price, but the whole book must cover it.

concepts.title: The price and margin waterfall
concepts.syllabus_text: A price and margin waterfall shows how discounts, rebates, freight, service, and other deductions reduce list price to pocket price and pocket margin.
concepts.one_liner: Step from list price down through every deduction to what you actually keep: pocket price.
concepts.explainer: List price is rarely what you earn. On-invoice deductions (standard and negotiated discounts) take you to invoice price. Off-invoice items (rebates, free freight, extended payment terms, co-op marketing, special service) take you to pocket price. Subtract variable cost to get pocket margin. Off-invoice items are often booked in other cost centres, so nobody sees the total leakage until someone draws the waterfall per customer or deal.
concepts.example: List 100 - discount 8 = invoice 92. Then rebate 3, payment terms 1.50, freight 2, co-op marketing 1.50 = pocket price 84. With cost 60, pocket margin is 24, not the 40 the list price suggests.

research_questions: How does your chosen business define gross margin and contribution margin?
Which costs vary with one additional sale, and which costs stay fixed in the relevant decision period?
Where does commercial leakage occur between list price and realized pocket price?
Which return measure would finance use to approve a pricing initiative?

worked_example.title: Week 1 exercise, worked
worked_example.setup: Price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units, fixed cost 250,000.
steps: Baseline: unit contribution 40, total contribution 400,000, operating profit 150,000.
+5% price: price 105, unit contribution 45.
Break-even volume = 10,000 x 40 / 45 = 8,889 units, a loss of 11.1%.
worked_example.takeaway: The increase pays unless you lose more than about 11% of volume. Fixed costs don't change the answer because they don't change with the decision.

weeks.title: Demand and elasticity
weeks.outcome: Explain how customer demand responds to price and use elasticity to evaluate the financial risk of a price change.
weeks.summary: Elasticity turns 'customers might leave' into a number you can put in a model. This week covers own-price, cross-price and income elasticity, how to estimate them, why estimates differ by segment and time horizon, and why a sales change after a price change is not automatically caused by the price.

concepts.title: The demand curve
concepts.syllabus_text: The demand curve describes the relationship between price and quantity, holding other material factors constant.
concepts.one_liner: Price vs quantity, with everything else held still - which real data never does.
concepts.explainer: A demand curve answers: if only the price changed, how many units would customers buy? 'Holding other factors constant' is the hard part. In real data, income, competitor prices, promotions, seasonality and stock availability all move at the same time as price. Moving along the curve (a price change) is different from the curve shifting (demand itself rising or falling). Confusing the two is the root of most bad elasticity estimates.
concepts.example: Ice-cream sales rise in summer even if you raise prices. That is the curve shifting out, not customers liking higher prices.

concepts.title: Own-price elasticity
concepts.syllabus_text: Own price elasticity measures the percentage change in quantity associated with a one percent change in price.
concepts.one_liner: Elasticity = % change in quantity / % change in price. Usually negative.
concepts.explainer: An elasticity of -2 means a 1% price rise loses about 2% of volume. If the absolute value is above 1, demand is elastic: volume moves more than price, so raising price cuts revenue. Below 1, demand is inelastic: raising price raises revenue. But revenue is not profit. Even elastic demand can make a price rise profitable if margins are thin, because the units you lose were barely profitable. Compare the elasticity to the break-even elasticity from your margin.
concepts.example: At elasticity -0.5, a 10% rise loses about 5% of volume and revenue rises about 4.5%. At -2.0, it loses about 20% and revenue falls about 12%.

concepts.title: Cross-price and income elasticity
concepts.syllabus_text: Cross price elasticity helps identify substitutes and complements. Income elasticity helps explain exposure to economic cycles.
concepts.one_liner: Cross-price shows which products compete or go together; income elasticity shows recession exposure.
concepts.explainer: Cross-price elasticity is the % change in demand for A when B's price changes 1%. Positive means substitutes (B gets dearer, people switch to A). Negative means complements (B gets dearer, people buy less of both). Within your own range this tells you about cannibalisation. Income elasticity is the % change in demand per 1% change in customer income. High positive values mean demand rises fast in booms and falls hard in downturns.
concepts.example: If a competitor's price rises 10% and your volume rises 4%, cross-price elasticity is +0.4: you are substitutes.

concepts.title: Elasticity is not one number
concepts.syllabus_text: Elasticity can differ by segment, channel, product, season, price level, and time horizon.
concepts.one_liner: Different customers, channels and horizons respond differently - a single average hides that.
concepts.explainer: Customers with good alternatives and low switching costs are more elastic. Online channels where comparison is easy tend to be more elastic than relationship-led channels. Elasticity usually rises (in absolute terms) at higher price levels and over longer horizons, because customers take time to notice, search and switch. A blended average can make a price rise look safe overall while it drives away a valuable, price-sensitive segment.
concepts.example: Short-run elasticity after a petrol price rise is low; over years people buy smaller cars, so the long-run response is much bigger.

concepts.title: Correlation is not price effect
concepts.syllabus_text: Observed sales changes are not automatically caused by price because promotions, availability, competitors, and seasonality also move demand.
concepts.one_liner: Before blaming (or crediting) price, rule out promotions, stock-outs, competitors and season.
concepts.explainer: Firms often set prices in response to demand: raising them when demand is strong, discounting when it's weak. That makes price and volume move together for reasons other than cause and effect, biasing naive estimates towards zero or even making them positive. This is called endogeneity. You need controls for the other drivers, a comparison group, or a controlled test (Week 8) before claiming a causal elasticity.
concepts.example: A retailer raised prices in December and sales went up. That's Christmas demand, not a positive elasticity.
concepts.lending_lens: In lending, price also changes who accepts. If riskier merchants are more willing to accept a higher factor rate, a price rise can keep take-up steady while worsening the loss rate of the book. Watch mix and losses, not just volume.

research_questions: What evidence suggests your product is elastic or inelastic?
Which customer segments have meaningful alternatives and switching ability?
How quickly can customers change behavior after a price increase?
Which historical variables must be controlled before treating a sales change as a price effect?

worked_example.title: Arc elasticity and the break-even test
worked_example.setup: Price moves from 10 to 12; volume moves from 1,000 to 850. Contribution margin at the old price is 40%.
steps: % change in quantity (midpoint) = (850 - 1,000) / 925 = -16.2%.
% change in price (midpoint) = (12 - 10) / 11 = +18.2%.
Arc elasticity = -16.2 / 18.2 = -0.89.
Break-even volume loss for a 20% rise at 40% margin = 0.20 / 0.60 = 33.3%.
Actual loss was 15%, well inside 33.3%, so contribution rose.
worked_example.takeaway: Compare the volume you actually lose with the volume you can afford to lose. The elasticity only matters relative to your margin.

weeks.title: Customer value and willingness to pay
weeks.outcome: Estimate a defensible price range using customer value, willingness to pay research, and evidence about alternatives.
weeks.summary: Cost sets the floor and value sets the ceiling. This week is about estimating the ceiling: economic value to the customer, how willingness to pay is distributed, which research method answers which question, and why what customers say often differs from what they do.

concepts.title: Economic value to the customer (EVC)
concepts.syllabus_text: Economic value to the customer starts with the price of the next best alternative and adjusts for meaningful differentiation value.
concepts.one_liner: EVC = price of the next best alternative + what makes you better - what makes you worse.
concepts.explainer: Start with what the customer would pay for their best alternative (the reference value). Add positive differentiation value: measurable benefits you deliver that the alternative doesn't (time saved, revenue gained, risk avoided). Subtract negative differentiation value: things that are worse (switching cost, longer setup, missing features). The result is the most a rational, informed customer should pay. Pricing at EVC leaves them indifferent, so you normally price somewhere between the alternative and EVC, sharing the value.
concepts.example: Competitor costs 10k a year. Your product saves 4k of staff time but needs 1k of extra training. EVC = 10 + 4 - 1 = 13k. A price around 11-12k gives the customer a clear reason to switch.
concepts.lending_lens: For an SME the alternatives might be an overdraft, a term loan, a card, another revenue-based funder, or not borrowing. Positive differentiation: speed, repayments that flex with sales, no fixed term. Negative: higher total cost.

concepts.title: Willingness to pay is a distribution
concepts.syllabus_text: Willingness to pay is a distribution, not a single market number.
concepts.one_liner: Every customer has a different maximum price - think in curves, not single numbers.
concepts.explainer: Different customers value the same product differently. Lined up from highest to lowest willingness to pay, they form your demand curve. Any single price loses customers below it and leaves money on the table with customers above it. That gap is why segmentation, tiers and fences (Week 4) exist. Research should estimate the shape of the distribution, not just an average.
concepts.example: If WTP ranges from 50 to 200, pricing at 100 loses everyone below 100 and undercharges everyone who would have paid up to 200.

concepts.title: WTP research methods
concepts.syllabus_text: Gabor Granger, Van Westendorp, conjoint analysis, and discrete choice methods answer different research questions.
concepts.one_liner: Pick the method by the decision: price point, acceptable range, or feature trade-off.
concepts.explainer: Gabor-Granger asks whether you would buy at a series of prices, giving a simple demand curve for a known product. Van Westendorp asks four questions (too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, too expensive) to find an acceptable range; it says nothing about how many will buy. Conjoint analysis has respondents trade off product profiles so you can estimate the value of each feature, including price. Discrete choice (choice-based conjoint) asks them to pick between realistic options, including 'none', which is closest to a real purchase.
concepts.example: Setting the price of an existing product: Gabor-Granger. Deciding what goes in a premium tier: conjoint. Sanity-checking a range for a new concept: Van Westendorp.

concepts.title: Stated vs revealed preference
concepts.syllabus_text: Stated preference can diverge from purchase behavior. Research design should reduce hypothetical bias and strategic responses.
concepts.one_liner: People say they'd pay more than they do - and buyers sometimes lowball on purpose.
concepts.explainer: Hypothetical bias: with no money on the line, respondents overstate what they'd pay. Strategic response: savvy buyers (especially B2B procurement) understate WTP to push your price down. Reduce both with realistic choice tasks instead of direct 'what would you pay' questions, including a 'none' option, reminding respondents of their budget, and validating survey results against real purchase data or a small live test.
concepts.example: A survey says 60% would pay 20. At launch, 15% take it. That gap is typical of hypothetical bias.

concepts.title: Value communication
concepts.syllabus_text: Value communication affects realized willingness to pay, especially when the benefit is unfamiliar or difficult to quantify.
concepts.one_liner: Customers pay for value they can see, not value that exists.
concepts.explainer: EVC is what an informed customer would pay. Real customers often don't know how much time you save or risk you remove, so their perceived value sits below economic value. Quantified case studies, ROI calculators, trials and guarantees close that gap. This matters most for new categories or benefits that are indirect, delayed or hard to measure.
concepts.example: A tool that cuts invoice errors by 30% is worth more if sales can show the customer what errors currently cost them.

research_questions: What measurable customer outcome changes because of the product?
What is the next best alternative for each major segment?
Which value claims can be documented with operational or financial evidence?
Which research method matches the decision: price point, feature tradeoff, or package design?

worked_example.title: EVC for one segment
worked_example.setup: Next best alternative costs 10,000 a year. Your product saves 160 staff hours a year at 25/hour and avoids 1,000 of errors. It needs 1,000 of extra training and has 1,000 of one-off switching cost, spread over 2 years.
steps: Reference value: 10,000.
Positive differentiation: 160 x 25 = 4,000 time saved, plus 1,000 errors avoided = 5,000.
Negative differentiation: training 1,000, plus switching 1,000 / 2 years = 500. Total 1,500.
Price range: above 10,000 (no reason to cut below the alternative) and well below 13,500 (customer needs an incentive to switch).
worked_example.takeaway: Label each line as observed, calculated or assumed. The error-avoidance figure is usually the weakest evidence.

weeks.title: Segmentation and price architecture
weeks.outcome: Design prices, packages, and qualification rules that capture differences in customer value while remaining understandable and operable.
weeks.summary: Because willingness to pay varies, one price leaves money on the table. Price architecture - tiers, bundles, metrics and fences - lets different customers pay different amounts in a way that is fair, understandable and hard to game.

concepts.title: Useful pricing segments
concepts.syllabus_text: Useful pricing segments differ in willingness to pay, cost to serve, behavior, or value received and can be identified during a transaction.
concepts.one_liner: A segment is only useful for pricing if it differs AND you can tell who's in it at the point of sale.
concepts.explainer: Marketing segments based on attitudes ('innovators', 'price-conscious') are hard to use in pricing because you can't see them on a quote. Pricing segments must be observable when the deal happens: company size, industry, channel, order volume, contract length, usage, tenure. They must also differ in something that matters to price - willingness to pay, cost to serve, behaviour or value received. If either test fails, the segment can't support a different price.
concepts.example: 'Values premium service' is not usable. 'Requests same-day delivery' is, because it's on the order.

concepts.title: Price fences
concepts.syllabus_text: Price fences define who qualifies for a price or offer and reduce uncontrolled arbitrage.
concepts.one_liner: Fences are the rules that stop high-WTP customers buying at the low price.
concepts.explainer: Fences come in a few types. Product fences: different versions (basic vs pro). Buyer fences: who you are (student, new customer, small business). Transaction fences: when or how you buy (advance purchase, volume, annual commitment, channel). Controlled availability: limited stock at a price. A good fence is easy to verify, hard to fake and feels fair. A weak fence (self-declared status with no check) leaks revenue through misrepresentation or resale.
concepts.example: Airline advance-purchase fares fence out business travellers, who book late and won't commit early.

concepts.title: Pricing models
concepts.syllabus_text: Good better best tiers, bundles, usage pricing, subscriptions, and two part tariffs suit different value and consumption patterns.
concepts.one_liner: Match the model to how customers get value: tiers, bundles, usage, subscription or fixed + usage.
concepts.explainer: Good-better-best tiers let customers self-select by WTP. Bundles sell items together; they work best when customers value the parts differently (negatively correlated WTP). Usage pricing charges per unit consumed and scales with value. Subscriptions charge for ongoing access. A two-part tariff combines a fixed fee with a usage price, capturing value from both light and heavy users. The value metric - what you charge per - should grow with the value the customer gets.
concepts.example: Customer A values X at 8 and Y at 3; B values X at 5 and Y at 6. Best separate prices earn 16; a bundle at 11 earns 22.

concepts.title: Architecture should guide, not confuse
concepts.syllabus_text: Product and price architecture should guide customers toward a suitable offer without creating unnecessary complexity.
concepts.one_liner: A good line-up makes the right choice obvious; too many options paralyse buyers and sales.
concepts.explainer: Tiers should have a clear target customer each and a clear reason to upgrade. Anchoring and the compromise effect mean a premium tier makes the middle look reasonable, and many customers pick the middle. But beyond three or four options, choice overload slows decisions and sales reps start improvising. Avoid a deliberately crippled entry tier - customers feel tricked and it damages trust.
concepts.example: Three tiers where 60% of customers pick the middle one usually means the architecture is doing its job.

concepts.title: Fairness, transparency and law
concepts.syllabus_text: Fairness, transparency, and legal constraints limit how segmentation and personalized pricing should be implemented.
concepts.one_liner: Price differences must be explainable, fair and legal - not based on protected characteristics.
concepts.explainer: Customers accept price differences tied to something they control or understand (volume, timing, features). They resent differences that feel arbitrary or exploitative. Law restricts discrimination on protected characteristics, and some sectors have rules on fair value and transparency. Even legal personalisation can damage trust if discovered. Test every fence by asking: could we explain this to a customer and a regulator?
concepts.example: A volume discount is easy to defend. Charging more because a customer's device suggests they're wealthy is not.
concepts.lending_lens: Risk-based pricing tiers should use data observable at application (trading history, card turnover, sector) and be explainable. Avoid proxies for protected characteristics.

research_questions: Which observable variable can separate customers with different willingness to pay?
Could customers easily misrepresent their segment or resell across segments?
Which features belong in each tier, and which are merely expensive to serve?
How many options can sales and customers understand without confusion?

worked_example.title: Why bundling works
worked_example.setup: Two customers. A values X at 8 and Y at 3. B values X at 5 and Y at 6.
steps: Price X separately: at 5 both buy (10); at 8 only A buys (8). Best = 10.
Price Y separately: at 3 both buy (6); at 6 only B buys (6). Best = 6.
Total from separate pricing = 16.
Bundle: A values it at 11, B at 11. Price the bundle at 11 and both buy = 22.
Bundling adds 6 (+37.5%) because the two customers' preferences offset each other.
worked_example.takeaway: Bundling captures more value when WTPs are negatively correlated. If both customers valued both items similarly, bundling would add little.

weeks.title: Competition and market strategy
weeks.outcome: Use competitor evidence without reducing the pricing decision to automatic price matching.
weeks.summary: Competitor prices are evidence, not instructions. This week covers market structure, comparing offers like-for-like, basic game theory, why price wars destroy value, how to diagnose whether a problem is really about price, and the legal lines around competitor information.

concepts.title: Market structure and pricing power
concepts.syllabus_text: Market structure influences pricing power, likely reactions, and the value of differentiation.
concepts.one_liner: How many rivals and how different you are decide how much room you have on price.
concepts.explainer: Perfect competition: identical products, many sellers, no pricing power. Monopolistic competition: many sellers with differentiated products, so some power from differentiation. Oligopoly: a few big players who watch and react to each other, so every price move invites a response. Monopoly: one seller, maximum power, often regulated. The more differentiated you are and the fewer close rivals, the more your price depends on your value rather than theirs.
concepts.example: UK grocery is an oligopoly: a price cut by one large chain is quickly matched, so permanent share gains from price are rare.

concepts.title: Comparing like with like
concepts.syllabus_text: A competitor price is informative only when the offer, customer, transaction terms, and channel are comparable.
concepts.one_liner: Normalise before you compare - headline prices hide different offers, terms and customers.
concepts.explainer: A competitor's list price can be cheaper while their total cost to the customer is higher, or their offer smaller. Normalise for package size, included features, service level, contract length, payment terms, discounts and fees, and channel. Also check whether they target the same customers. An unadjusted list-price comparison is one of the most common reasons companies cut prices they didn't need to cut.
concepts.example: Competitor A is 10% cheaper but excludes onboarding and support and requires a 3-year contract. Normalised, they may be more expensive.
concepts.lending_lens: A competitor quoting a 1.20 factor vs your 1.28 isn't comparable until you check holdback %, fees, early-settlement discounts, advance size, speed and eligibility.

concepts.title: Game theory in pricing
concepts.syllabus_text: Game theory helps frame repeated interaction, credible commitments, entry, retaliation, and price leadership.
concepts.one_liner: Pricing is a repeated game: today's move shapes tomorrow's reaction.
concepts.explainer: In a one-off 'prisoner's dilemma', each firm is tempted to cut price, and both end up worse off. But competitors meet again and again, so reputations matter: firms that respond predictably to undercutting (tit-for-tat) discourage it. Credible commitments - like capacity or a publicly stated policy - change what rivals expect. Incumbents may price to deter entry. In some markets one firm acts as price leader and others follow. Use these ideas to predict reactions, not to coordinate with rivals.
concepts.example: If you cut price 10% and your rival always matches within a week, you gain almost no share and both lose margin.

concepts.title: Price wars
concepts.syllabus_text: Price wars often destroy value when firms react to visible prices without diagnosing the commercial cause of share loss.
concepts.one_liner: Diagnose why you lost share before cutting price - it's often not price at all.
concepts.explainer: Share loss can come from product gaps, stock-outs, service problems, a weak sales team, or losing a channel. Cutting price for any of those reasons sacrifices margin without fixing the cause, and invites retaliation. When responding to a competitor cut, compare: lost contribution from matching vs lost contribution from the volume you'd lose by not matching. Often a targeted response (specific segments or accounts) beats a broad one.
concepts.example: Price 100, cost 60, 10,000 units. Competitor cuts 10%. Matching keeps volume but contribution falls to 300k. Not matching breaks even unless you lose more than 25% of volume.

concepts.title: Competition law
concepts.syllabus_text: Competition law and antitrust rules require caution around communications, signaling, parity, resale pricing, and competitor information.
concepts.one_liner: Never discuss future pricing with competitors; be careful with signalling, parity clauses and resale price rules.
concepts.explainer: Agreeing prices with competitors (cartels) is illegal and can be criminal. Even sharing future pricing intentions, or exchanging competitively sensitive information through a third party, can breach the law. Public 'signalling' of intended price moves can raise concerns. Fixing the price at which resellers must sell (resale price maintenance) is usually prohibited. Price parity / most-favoured-nation clauses get regulatory scrutiny. Public competitor prices are fine to use. When unsure, involve legal - and know where those review points are.
concepts.example: Chatting to a competitor at a conference about 'where rates are going next quarter' is a red line.

research_questions: What market role does the business want: premium leader, parity player, disruptor, or focused specialist?
Which competitor moves would materially change the recommendation?
What evidence distinguishes a price problem from a product, availability, service, or sales problem?
Which competitive information can be collected and used lawfully in your jurisdiction and industry?

worked_example.title: Match or hold?
worked_example.setup: Your price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units. A competitor cuts their price 10%.
steps: Baseline contribution: 10,000 x 40 = 400,000.
Match (price 90): unit contribution 30. Even if volume holds, contribution = 300,000.
Hold (price 100): contribution = units retained x 40.
Holding is better unless units fall below 300,000 / 40 = 7,500 - a 25% loss.
Next step: estimate how many customers actually switch, by segment. If only one segment is at risk, a targeted response protects it without repricing everyone.
worked_example.takeaway: Matching is expensive. It's only right if you'd otherwise lose more volume than the break-even.

weeks.title: Transactional pricing and sales execution
weeks.outcome: Improve realized price by controlling discounts, rebates, exceptions, and deal economics while supporting effective selling.
weeks.summary: The price you set is not the price you get. This week is about the gap: waterfalls, pocket price bands, discount corridors, approval rules, sales incentives and negotiation. It's often the fastest source of margin improvement because no list price has to change.

concepts.title: Pocket price beats list price
concepts.syllabus_text: List price matters less than pocket price when discounts and off invoice deductions vary widely.
concepts.one_liner: When discounts vary deal by deal, the list price tells you little - pocket price is what counts.
concepts.explainer: If every customer gets a different mix of discounts, rebates and terms, list price becomes a starting point for negotiation rather than the price. Plot pocket price for similar customers buying similar products and you usually see a wide spread - the pocket price band. That spread rarely lines up with deal size or customer value; it often reflects which rep handled the deal or how hard the customer pushed.
concepts.example: Two customers of similar size buy the same volume. One pays a pocket price of 78, the other 91. The 13-point gap is negotiation, not value.

concepts.title: Finding leakage with the waterfall
concepts.syllabus_text: A price waterfall identifies leakage by customer, salesperson, product, channel, and deduction type.
concepts.one_liner: Slice the waterfall by rep, customer, product and channel to see exactly where price leaks.
concepts.explainer: The Week 1 waterfall becomes a diagnostic tool when you cut it by dimension. By rep: who discounts most for similar deals. By customer: who gets rebates they don't earn. By deduction type: which item (payment terms, freight, promotions) grows fastest. By channel: where partners take more than agreed. The goal is to separate earned deductions (tied to a customer commitment) from habitual leakage.
concepts.example: Freight is waived on 70% of small orders, though policy says only above 500. That's a process leak worth fixing before any price change.
concepts.lending_lens: Lending leakage: commission overrides to brokers or partners, fees waived at renewal, unpriced early-settlement discounts, and advances rounded up beyond the approved amount.

concepts.title: Making policy operational
concepts.syllabus_text: Discount corridors, floors, approval thresholds, and exception codes make pricing policy operational.
concepts.one_liner: Corridors, floors, approval levels and exception codes turn a pricing policy into rules reps can follow.
concepts.explainer: A discount corridor sets the normal range for a type of deal (by segment, size, term). Green: rep can approve. Amber: manager approval. Red: deal desk or finance. A floor price is the level below which no deal goes. Exception codes record why an out-of-policy deal was approved ('competitive', 'strategic logo', 'volume commitment'), so you can learn from patterns. Without these, policy lives in a slide deck and nowhere else.
concepts.example: Corridor: 0-10% green, 10-15% amber, above 15% deal desk. An 18% request goes to the deal desk with a reason code.

concepts.title: Sales incentives
concepts.syllabus_text: Sales incentives can undermine pricing when compensation rewards revenue or volume without regard to contribution.
concepts.one_liner: Pay reps on revenue and they'll discount to close; pay on margin and they'll defend price.
concepts.explainer: If commission is a % of revenue, a 10% discount reduces the rep's pay by only 10% of commission but may cut the company's contribution by 25% or more. Reps rationally trade margin for speed and certainty. Fixes include paying on gross margin or contribution, adding a price-realisation multiplier, or reducing commission on discounted deals. Changing incentives is usually more effective than tightening approvals alone.
concepts.example: At a 40% margin, a 10% discount needs 33% more volume to break even - but costs the rep only 10% of their commission on that deal.

concepts.title: Give-get negotiation
concepts.syllabus_text: A strong negotiation process exchanges concessions for customer commitments instead of granting discounts without return.
concepts.one_liner: Never give a concession without getting something back.
concepts.explainer: Every discount should buy something of value: higher volume, longer term, upfront payment, faster decision, a case study, auto-renewal, reduced scope or service. Prepare the 'get' list before the negotiation. Trade small concessions for big commitments, concede slowly, and use non-price variables (payment terms, service level, implementation timing) before touching price. This protects margin and teaches customers that pushing on price alone doesn't work.
concepts.example: 'We can do 5% if you commit to 24 months and pay annually upfront.'

research_questions: Which deductions are earned by customer behavior and which are habitual leakage?
How much margin variance exists within comparable transactions?
Which exceptions should sales approve independently and which require a deal desk?
What nonprice variables can be traded during negotiation?

weeks.exercise: Create a price waterfall from list price to pocket margin using at least five deduction types. worked_example.title: An illustrative MCA deal waterfall
worked_example.setup: Advance 50,000 at a 1.30 factor rate (illustrative numbers, not any lender's actual economics).
steps: Total repayable = 65,000. Gross fee = 15,000.
Partner/broker commission at 8% of advance: -4,000.
Expected credit loss at 5% of repayable: -3,250.
Cost of funds (average balance ~half the advance for ~9 months at 10%/yr): -1,875.
Underwriting and servicing: -500.
worked_example.takeaway: A third of the headline fee survives to contribution. Commission and loss assumptions move the answer far more than small factor-rate changes.

weeks.title: Revenue management and dynamic pricing
weeks.outcome: Use demand forecasts, capacity, inventory, and timing to make prices responsive without losing commercial control.
weeks.summary: When capacity is fixed and perishable, the question changes from 'what price?' to 'which customers get the capacity, at what price, and when?'. This week covers revenue management, dynamic vs personalised pricing, markdowns, and the guardrails that stop an optimiser damaging trust.

concepts.title: When revenue management works
concepts.syllabus_text: Revenue management is most useful when capacity is constrained, inventory expires, demand varies, and customers book at different times.
concepts.one_liner: Fixed, perishable capacity + variable demand + customers booking at different times = revenue management territory.
concepts.explainer: Airlines and hotels are the classic cases: an empty seat or room tonight is worth nothing tomorrow, adding capacity is slow and expensive, demand swings, and price-sensitive leisure customers book early while less sensitive business customers book late. Revenue management sells the same capacity at different prices through booking classes, and decides how much capacity to protect for later, higher-paying demand. Without those conditions, simpler pricing usually works better.
concepts.example: A hotel holds back rooms from the discount channel on weekdays near a conference, expecting late corporate bookings at higher rates.
concepts.lending_lens: Funding capacity works a bit like perishable inventory. When capital is constrained, each advance has an opportunity cost: allocate it to deals with the best risk-adjusted return per pound, not the most volume.

concepts.title: Dynamic vs personalised pricing
concepts.syllabus_text: Dynamic pricing changes the offer based on market conditions. Personalized pricing changes the offer based on information about the customer. The risks differ.
concepts.one_liner: Dynamic = price moves with market conditions. Personalised = price moves with who you are. Different risks.
concepts.explainer: Dynamic pricing reacts to demand, time, inventory or competitors; everyone sees the same price at the same moment. Customers broadly accept it when the logic is visible (peak vs off-peak). Personalised pricing uses data about the individual (history, location, device) so two people see different prices at the same time. It carries bigger fairness, transparency and legal risk, and can destroy trust if discovered, even when it's legal.
concepts.example: Surge pricing during a storm is dynamic. Showing a higher price to someone whose browsing suggests urgency is personalised.

concepts.title: Markdown optimisation
concepts.syllabus_text: Markdown optimization balances margin against sell through and leftover inventory risk.
concepts.one_liner: Mark down too early and you give away margin; too late and you're left with unsold stock.
concepts.explainer: For seasonal or perishable stock, the question is when and how deep to discount. Holding price protects margin on what sells but risks leftover stock that's worth little. Discounting earlier sells more but at lower margin. Compare expected total contribution, including salvage value of leftovers, across markdown paths. Sell-through (% of stock sold) is the key leading indicator.
concepts.example: 100 units left, two weeks to go. Holding at 50 sells 60 (3,000; 40 units scrapped). Marking down to 35 sells 95 (3,325). The markdown wins if leftovers are worth less than the difference.

concepts.title: Optimal on paper vs in practice
concepts.syllabus_text: Forecast error, competitor action, cancellations, and operational constraints can make a mathematically optimal price commercially weak.
concepts.one_liner: The model's optimum assumes its forecast is right - real-world error, rivals and operations can break it.
concepts.explainer: An optimiser is only as good as its demand forecast. Forecasts are wrong, competitors react, customers cancel or no-show, and operations can't always deliver what the model assumes. Test recommendations under low, expected and high demand. Prefer prices that are robust across scenarios over ones that are optimal only in the base case. Also check that revenue-maximising and profit-maximising answers agree; they differ when variable costs matter.
concepts.example: Price 8 sells 1,500 (revenue 12,000). Price 12 sells 900 (revenue 10,800). With variable cost 5, contribution is 4,500 vs 6,300 - the 'lower revenue' price is better.

concepts.title: Guardrails
concepts.syllabus_text: Guardrails should address customer fairness, transparency, volatility, brand, and operational feasibility.
concepts.one_liner: Set limits the algorithm can't cross: floors, ceilings, max change per period, fairness rules.
concepts.explainer: Guardrails keep automated pricing within commercially acceptable bounds. Typical ones: minimum margin or floor price, maximum price, maximum % change per day or week, no price rises during emergencies, consistent prices across channels where customers would notice, and rules against using sensitive data. They trade a little theoretical revenue for trust, brand protection and fewer embarrassing headlines.
concepts.example: A rule capping daily price changes at 10% and freezing prices during a declared emergency.

research_questions: Does the chosen business have perishable capacity or inventory?
Which demand signals arrive early enough to change price or availability?
How would customers react to prices changing across time, channel, or device?
What minimum margin, maximum change, or rate limit should the system enforce?

worked_example.title: Littlewood's rule: how many seats to protect
worked_example.setup: Two fares: full 300, discount 100. Discount customers book first. How many seats should you hold back for full-fare customers?
steps: Selling one more seat at discount earns 100 for certain.
Holding that seat earns 300 only if full-fare demand exceeds the seats already protected.
Keep protecting seats while P(full-fare demand > protected seats) x 300 >= 100.
That means protect while the probability is at least 1/3.
If there's a 40% chance full-fare demand exceeds 20 seats, protect the 21st too; at 30%, sell it at discount.
worked_example.takeaway: The protection level depends on the fare ratio and the full-fare demand forecast - not on filling the plane.

weeks.title: Pricing analytics and experimentation
weeks.outcome: Design analysis that separates the effect of price from other changes and produces evidence suitable for a business decision.
weeks.summary: Most pricing data is observational and confounded. This week covers what a usable pricing dataset contains, why regression alone can mislead, how to run tests or quasi-experiments when randomisation is hard, and how to write a measurement plan with a decision rule before you see the results.

concepts.title: A useful pricing dataset
concepts.syllabus_text: A useful pricing dataset includes realized price, units, product, customer, time, channel, promotions, availability, cost, and relevant market variables.
concepts.one_liner: Realised price, units, product, customer, time, channel, promos, availability, cost, market - or you can't separate price from everything else.
concepts.explainer: Elasticity estimates need the realised price customers actually paid, not list price. They also need the other things that move demand, so you can control for them: promotions, stock-outs, seasonality, competitor prices, channel. Cost is needed to translate volume effects into profit. Missing any of these usually means the estimate silently absorbs the effect of the missing variable.
concepts.example: If stock-out days aren't recorded, a period with high prices and empty shelves looks like extreme price sensitivity.

concepts.title: Limits of regression
concepts.syllabus_text: Regression can control for observed variables, but omitted variables and reverse causality may still bias elasticity estimates.
concepts.one_liner: Regression only controls what you measured - omitted variables and reverse causality still bias it.
concepts.explainer: Omitted variable bias: something you didn't measure (a competitor's promotion, a marketing campaign) affects both price and volume. Reverse causality: you set price because of demand, so demand partly causes price, not just the other way round. Both bias the price coefficient, usually towards zero. Adding more controls helps only for the variables you can observe. For a causal answer you need variation in price that isn't driven by demand - ideally a test.
concepts.example: Regions with strong demand got price rises first. Regression shows small elasticity, but that's because demand caused the price, not because customers don't care.

concepts.title: Randomised price tests
concepts.syllabus_text: Randomized tests strengthen causal inference when they are feasible, ethical, and commercially controlled.
concepts.one_liner: Randomise who gets which price, and differences in outcome are caused by price.
concepts.explainer: Random assignment makes test and control groups alike on average in everything except price, so the difference in outcomes is the price effect. Decide the unit of assignment (customer, store, region, time period). Watch for contamination: customers seeing both prices, sales reps working both groups. Price tests also raise fairness concerns - customers comparing notes may object - so many firms test on new customers, new products, or across regions rather than individuals.
concepts.example: Randomly assign new applicants to one of two price points for four weeks and compare conversion and contribution per applicant.
concepts.lending_lens: Lending tests have slow outcomes: losses and repayment speed take months to appear. Use leading indicators (take-up, early repayment velocity, early arrears) with pre-agreed guardrails, and check fairness and any regulatory rules first.

concepts.title: Quasi-experiments
concepts.syllabus_text: Matched markets, difference in differences, synthetic controls, and phased rollouts can help when individual randomization is impractical.
concepts.one_liner: When you can't randomise, build a credible comparison group instead.
concepts.explainer: Matched markets: change price in some markets and compare to similar unchanged markets. Difference-in-differences: compare the change over time in the treated group with the change in the control group; this removes shared trends but assumes the groups would have moved in parallel without the change. Synthetic control: build a weighted blend of untreated units that tracks the treated unit before the change. Phased (staggered) rollout: introduce the change in waves so later waves act as controls for earlier ones.
concepts.example: Treatment region conversion 20% to 18%; control 21% to 20%. DiD effect = -2 - (-1) = -1 percentage point.

concepts.title: The measurement plan
concepts.syllabus_text: The measurement plan should specify a decision rule, minimum detectable effect, guardrails, and how profit will be calculated.
concepts.one_liner: Write down what result means launch, revise or reject - before you look at the data.
concepts.explainer: A good plan states the decision it supports, the primary metric (ideally incremental contribution, not conversion alone), the minimum detectable effect (the smallest effect worth detecting, which drives sample size), guardrail metrics that would stop the test (complaints, churn, loss rates), the duration, and the decision rule. Pre-committing stops people moving the goalposts after seeing the numbers.
concepts.example: Rule of thumb for 80% power at 5% significance: n per group is about 16 x p(1-p) / d^2. Baseline 20% conversion, detect 2 points: about 6,400 per group.

research_questions: What decision will the analysis support and what evidence would change that decision?
Could demand conditions have caused both the observed price and the observed sales result?
Which customers or markets can serve as a credible comparison group?
What leading indicators and guardrails should be monitored before the final profit outcome is available?

worked_example.title: Why conversion isn't enough
worked_example.setup: Control: price 100, variable cost 60, 1,000 visitors, 20% convert. Test: price 110, 1,000 visitors, 17% convert.
steps: Conversion fell 3 points - looks like a loss.
Control contribution: 200 sales x 40 = 8,000.
Test contribution: 170 sales x 50 = 8,500.
Incremental contribution per visitor: +0.50 for the test.
Decision depends on whether that difference is bigger than the noise and whether guardrails (complaints, churn) held.
worked_example.takeaway: Judge price tests on contribution per eligible customer. Conversion and revenue can point the wrong way.

weeks.title: Commercial implementation and governance
weeks.outcome: Convert a pricing recommendation into a launch plan that sales, finance, operations, product, and leadership can execute and monitor.
weeks.summary: Good pricing decisions fail in execution all the time. This week covers launch logistics, customer communication, sales enablement, decision rights and exception governance, and a scorecard that tells you whether a disappointing result came from the idea or the rollout.

concepts.title: Launch essentials
concepts.syllabus_text: Implementation needs a clear effective date, affected customers, transition rules, system changes, owners, and escalation paths.
concepts.one_liner: Effective date, who's affected, transition rules, systems, owners, escalation - or it isn't a plan.
concepts.explainer: Decide exactly when the new price applies and to whom: new customers, renewals, existing contracts. Set transition rules: grandfathering (existing customers keep old prices for a period), notice periods, and how in-flight quotes are honoured. List every system that must change (quoting, billing, CRM, websites, partner portals) and test before go-live. Every task needs a named owner, and there must be a clear route for problems on day one.
concepts.example: New prices for new applications from 1 March; existing customers move at their next renewal; quotes issued before 1 March honoured for 30 days.
concepts.lending_lens: Think in cohorts: new merchants, renewing merchants, and partners who present offers. Each may need different timing, messaging and system changes.

concepts.title: Customer communication
concepts.syllabus_text: Customer communication should explain the commercial change accurately and equip teams to discuss value without making unsupported claims.
concepts.one_liner: Explain the change honestly, link it to value, and don't let anyone promise what you can't prove.
concepts.explainer: Tell customers what changes, when, and why, in plain language. Link it to value delivered, not just your costs. Give enough notice to be fair (and meet any contractual terms). Customer-facing teams need approved messaging so they don't improvise claims ('this is the lowest price in the market') that can't be supported and may create legal or trust problems.
concepts.example: Better: 'From 1 March, the fee rises 4% to fund faster payouts, now same day.' Worse: 'Costs went up so prices go up.'

concepts.title: Sales enablement
concepts.syllabus_text: Sales enablement needs talk tracks, objection handling, approval rules, examples, and practice with realistic deals.
concepts.one_liner: Reps need words, answers to objections, the rules, examples and practice - not just an email.
concepts.explainer: A talk track gives reps a short, consistent way to explain the change. Objection handling prepares answers for the predictable pushback ('too expensive', 'competitor is cheaper', 'we've been loyal'). Reps need the updated approval rules and corridors, worked deal examples, and role-play practice before they face customers. Under-prepared reps fall back on discounting, which erases the price change.
concepts.example: Objection 'too expensive': acknowledge, ask what they're comparing against, reframe on outcomes, and only trade price for a commitment.

concepts.title: Governance and decision rights
concepts.syllabus_text: Governance defines decision rights for list prices, discounts, promotions, exceptions, and post launch corrections.
concepts.one_liner: Be clear who decides list prices, discounts, promotions, exceptions and corrections.
concepts.explainer: Without clear decision rights, pricing drifts: sales grants exceptions, marketing runs promotions, finance pushes back, and nobody owns the outcome. A RACI matrix (Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed) makes it explicit, with exactly one Accountable per decision. Exceptions should be logged with reasons and reviewed regularly; if the same exception keeps being approved, the policy is wrong and should change.
concepts.example: 40% of deals use the 'competitive' exception. That's not an exception any more - it's the real price, and the corridor needs revisiting.

concepts.title: Performance tracking
concepts.syllabus_text: Performance tracking should separate adoption, realized price, volume response, mix, customer retention, and financial return.
concepts.one_liner: Track each link in the chain separately, so you know whether the idea or the rollout failed.
concepts.explainer: If profit disappoints, you need to know why. Adoption: is the new price actually in the systems and on quotes? Realised price: did discounting erode it? Volume response: did customers react as predicted? Mix: did the customer or product mix shift? Retention: are existing customers leaving? Financial return: what's the net effect? If adoption or realisation failed, the hypothesis was never tested - that's implementation failure, not a bad idea.
concepts.example: List price rose 5% in the system, but realised price rose only 1% because reps offset it with discounts. Fix enablement and incentives before concluding the price rise failed.

research_questions: Which customers need notice, renewal treatment, grandfathering, or contract review?
Which systems and data fields must change before the effective date?
What will sales need to explain the change confidently and accurately?
Who can approve an exception and how will repeated exceptions change policy?
