worked_example.title: Reading a launch scorecard
worked_example.setup: Planned (at a 40% contribution margin): +5% realised price, -4% volume, +8% contribution. Month 2 actuals below.
steps: Adoption: 98% of quotes on new price list. OK.
Realised price: +1.5% vs +5% plan. Problem.
Volume: -2% vs -4% plan. Better than expected.
Exception log: 'competitive' code on 35% of deals, up from 10%.
Diagnosis: implementation failure (discounting offset), not a flawed hypothesis - customers reacted less than feared.
worked_example.takeaway: Without separate adoption and realisation lines, this would have looked like 'the price rise didn't work'.

weeks.title: Capstone pricing recommendation
weeks.outcome: Combine the weekly work into a recommendation that a commercial leadership team could approve, reject, or revise.
weeks.summary: The capstone pulls everything together into a decision someone can actually make. This week covers how to structure a decision-ready recommendation, present scenarios and sensitivities honestly, build a profit bridge, separate facts from assumptions, and set triggers to stop, adjust or expand after launch.

concepts.title: What makes a recommendation decision-ready
concepts.syllabus_text: A decision ready recommendation states the decision, financial effect, customer logic, evidence, operational plan, and material risks.
concepts.one_liner: Decision, money, customer logic, evidence, plan, risks - in that order, decision first.
concepts.explainer: Executives read the first page and decide whether to keep going. Lead with the decision you're asking for: the price change, scope, effective date and approval needed. Then the financial effect, why customers will accept it, the evidence behind your numbers, how it will be executed, and what could go wrong. This 'answer first' structure (often called the pyramid principle) respects the reader's time and makes the ask unmissable.
concepts.example: Slide 1: 'Approve a 4% factor-rate increase for new merchants in tiers B-C from 1 March. Expected +X contribution in year 1; downside break-even if take-up falls more than Y%.'

concepts.title: Scenarios and assumptions
concepts.syllabus_text: The base case should be accompanied by downside and upside scenarios and explicit assumptions.
concepts.one_liner: Show base, downside and upside - and the assumptions that move between them.
concepts.explainer: A single number hides uncertainty. Show a base case plus downside and upside cases, each driven by stated assumptions (elasticity, competitor reaction, adoption, cost). A sensitivity analysis (often shown as a tornado chart) shows which assumption moves the answer most. Pair it with the break-even condition: how bad must the key assumption be before the decision is wrong? Decision-makers trust honest ranges more than false precision.
concepts.example: 'We break even unless volume falls more than 11%. Our base case is -5%; the downside, assuming a competitor matches, is -9%.'

concepts.title: Learning after launch
concepts.syllabus_text: Implementation metrics and learning milestones matter because the initial estimate will be imperfect.
concepts.one_liner: Your estimate will be wrong - plan when you'll check and what would change your mind.
concepts.explainer: Build learning milestones into the plan: dates when you'll review leading indicators and pre-agreed triggers for each outcome. Stop if guardrails are breached (e.g. retention drops beyond a threshold). Adjust if a segment responds worse than expected. Expand if results beat the base case. This turns the recommendation from a one-off bet into a managed experiment and makes approval easier.
concepts.example: Week 4 review: if take-up in tier C falls more than 10%, revert tier C; if under 3%, extend to tier D.

concepts.title: Facts, estimates, assumptions and choices
concepts.syllabus_text: The recommendation should distinguish facts, estimates, assumptions, and management choices.
concepts.one_liner: Label each claim: fact, estimate, assumption or choice - so people know what to challenge.
concepts.explainer: Facts are observed and verifiable (last year's volume). Estimates are derived from data with uncertainty (elasticity of -1.4). Assumptions are judgements without strong data (competitors won't react for 6 months). Management choices are value calls (protecting share in a strategic segment). Mixing them up makes a recommendation look more certain than it is and hides where debate should focus.
concepts.example: 'Volume 10,000 (fact); elasticity -1.4 +/- 0.4 (estimate); no competitor response in Q1 (assumption); prioritise margin over share (choice).'

research_questions: What exact decision is being requested and by when?
Which assumption contributes most to the financial return and how can it be tested?
Who gains, who loses, and which customers or channels face the highest risk?
What early evidence would cause the team to stop, adjust, or expand the change?

resources.title: UVA and BCG Pricing Strategy Optimization
resources.note: Use the cases to compare your reasoning and recommendation structure.

resources.title: Columbia Business School Pricing Methodologies
resources.note: Optional reference for an integrated analytical and commercial pricing approach.

weeks.exercise: Finalize the capstone using the structure below. Ask a colleague or study partner to challenge the elasticity, cost, customer value, and implementation assumptions. Revise the recommendation after the challenge session.
weeks.portfolio_output: An eight to ten slide executive presentation and the supporting financial model. If you do not want to build slides, write a five page decision memo using the same structure.
self_check: The requested decision appears on the first page or slide.
The financial case reconciles from price and volume to contribution or operating profit.
The commercial plan is specific enough to execute and measure.

worked_example.title: A profit bridge from price and volume
worked_example.setup: Baseline: price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units, contribution 400,000. New: price 105, volume 9,300.
steps: Price effect = price change x new volume = 5 x 9,300 = +46,500.
Volume effect = volume change x old unit contribution = -700 x 40 = -28,000.
Net = +18,500, matching the new contribution of 418,500.
If there were mix or cost changes, they'd be separate bars.
worked_example.takeaway: A bridge shows leadership exactly where the money comes from and reconciles back to the model - which is what the scoring guide checks.

flashcards.back: Net price minus variable cost per unit. What each sale adds towards fixed costs and profit.
Margin = profit / price. Markup = profit / cost. Price 100, cost 60: margin 40%, markup 66.7%.
Markup = margin / (1 - margin). A 40% margin is a 66.7% markup.
Margin = markup / (1 + markup). A 50% markup is a 33.3% margin.

flashcards.front: Break-even volume change after a price change
flashcards.back: -dP / (CM% + dP), with dP and CM% as fractions of the old price. The volume you can lose (or must gain) for contribution to stay flat.

flashcards.front: Contribution margin 40%, price +5%. How much volume can you lose and break even?
Contribution margin 40%, price -5%. How much extra volume do you need to break even?
flashcards.back: 14.3%. 0.05 / (0.40 - 0.05). Cuts need more volume than increases can afford to lose.

flashcards.front: Why do price cuts need disproportionately more volume to pay off?
flashcards.back: The whole cut comes out of unit contribution. At a 40% margin, a 5% cut removes 1/8 of each unit's contribution, so you need about 14% more units just to stand still.
A cost that changes because of the decision. Sunk costs and unaffected fixed costs are irrelevant to a short-run pricing choice.

flashcards.front: When does fully allocated cost still matter?
flashcards.back: For reporting and long-run viability. Prices across the business must eventually cover fixed costs, or the business shrinks even if every deal is 'contribution positive'.
What you actually keep from a transaction after all on- and off-invoice deductions: discounts, rebates, freight, payment terms, promotions, extra service.
A chart stepping from list price through every deduction to pocket price and pocket margin. Shows where price leaks.

On-invoice appear on the bill (standard and negotiated discounts). Off-invoice happen later or elsewhere (rebates, free freight, extended terms, co-op marketing) and are often invisible in price reports.

flashcards.front: Waterfall leakage: pricing action vs process action?
flashcards.back: Policy-driven deductions (discount levels, rebate rates) need a pricing action. Execution failures (unbilled freight, rebates paid when targets weren't hit, payment terms not enforced) need a process fix.
Marn and Rosiello (HBR, 1992): for the average large company, a 1% price rise with no volume loss lifted operating profit by about 11%. Price is usually the biggest profit lever.

flashcards.front: Price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units, fixed cost 250k. Operating profit?
flashcards.back: 150k. Contribution 10,000 x 40 = 400k, minus 250k fixed.

flashcards.front: Same business (op. profit 150k). Price +1%, volume flat. % change in operating profit?
MCA: what is the 'price', and what actually drives the return?
flashcards.back: The factor rate sets the total fee, but the annualised return depends on how fast the holdback repays. Same factor, faster repayment = higher IRR.

flashcards.front: Why must a pricing recommendation state which measure it optimises?
flashcards.back: The revenue-maximising price is usually lower than the contribution-maximising one, and cash timing can differ again. Without a stated measure, two analysts can 'prove' opposite answers.
The relationship between price and quantity demanded, holding other factors constant (income, competitor prices, promotions, season).
% change in quantity / % change in price. Usually negative. -2 means a 1% price rise loses about 2% of volume.
Elastic (|E| > 1): volume moves more than price, so a price rise cuts revenue. Inelastic (|E| < 1): a price rise raises revenue.

flashcards.front: Elasticity -0.5 vs -2.0 in commercial terms (10% price rise)?
flashcards.back: -0.5: lose ~5% of volume, revenue up ~4.5%. -2.0: lose ~20% of volume, revenue down ~12%.
[(Q2 - Q1) / average Q] / [(P2 - P1) / average P]. Using midpoints gives the same answer whichever direction you measure.

flashcards.front: Price 10 to 12, quantity 1,000 to 850. Arc elasticity?

flashcards.back: ln(Q) = a + b ln(P) + controls. The coefficient b is the elasticity, assumed constant across prices.
% change in demand for A / % change in price of B. Positive = substitutes. Negative = complements.
% change in demand / % change in income. High positive values mean demand swings with the economic cycle.

flashcards.front: Why is long-run elasticity usually larger than short-run?
flashcards.back: Customers need time to notice, search, find substitutes and break contracts. The longer the horizon, the more of them switch.

flashcards.front: Sales fell after a price rise. Why isn't that proof of a price effect?
flashcards.back: Promotions, stock-outs, competitor moves or seasonality may also have changed. Without controls or a comparison group, you can't attribute the drop to price.

flashcards.front: Break-even elasticity for a price rise
flashcards.back: About break-even volume change / price change. Margin 40%, +5%: -11.1% / 5% = -2.2. If true elasticity is less negative than -2.2, the rise pays.
(P - MC) / P = -1 / E. At E = -2 the best margin is 50%; at E = -4 it's 25%. More elastic demand means thinner optimal margins.

flashcards.front: Why distrust an elasticity outside the observed price range?
flashcards.back: The curve can bend: price thresholds, competitor reactions and new substitutes kick in. Extrapolating assumes a shape you never observed.
Price is set in response to demand, so price and volume move together for non-causal reasons. Biases elasticity towards zero, or even positive.
Response to a temporary price cut. Inflated by stockpiling and pulling purchases forward, so it overstates the response to a permanent change.

flashcards.front: Lending: raise the factor rate and take-up barely moves. Is that a win?
flashcards.back: Not yet. Higher price can change who accepts (adverse selection). Check the risk mix and loss rates of accepted merchants, not just take-up.

flashcards.front: Can a price rise be profitable even when demand is elastic?
flashcards.back: Yes. Elastic means revenue falls, but if margins are thin, the lost units were barely profitable while every remaining unit earns more. Compare to break-even elasticity.
Price of the next best alternative + positive differentiation value - negative differentiation value.
The price of the customer's next best alternative. The starting point of an EVC estimate.
Positive: measurable benefits beyond the alternative (time, revenue, risk). Negative: ways you're worse (switching cost, setup time, missing features).

flashcards.front: Alternative costs 10k. You save 4k of labour but need 1k more training. EVC?

flashcards.back: At EVC the customer is indifferent. You need to share value to give a reason to switch and to cover their uncertainty about your claims.

flashcards.front: Why is WTP a distribution, not a number?
flashcards.back: Customers value the product differently. Any single price loses those below it and undercharges those above it - which is why segmentation and tiers exist.
Asks 'would you buy at price X?' across a series of prices. Builds a simple demand curve and revenue-maximising price for a known product.
Four questions: too cheap, a bargain, getting expensive, too expensive. Gives an acceptable price range. Doesn't measure purchase likelihood.
Respondents trade off product profiles. Estimates the value of each feature, including price, so you can work out WTP per feature and design packages.
Respondents choose between realistic options, including 'none'. Closest survey method to a real purchase decision.

flashcards.front: Match the method: set a price for an existing product / design tiers / early range check
flashcards.back: Existing product price point: Gabor-Granger. Tier and feature design: conjoint. Early range check for a new concept: Van Westendorp.
With no money on the line, people overstate what they'd pay. Reduce with realistic choices, a 'none' option, and validation against real behaviour.
Respondents deliberately understate WTP to keep prices low. Common with B2B buyers.

flashcards.front: Why does value communication change realised WTP?
flashcards.back: Customers pay for value they perceive. If a benefit is unfamiliar or hard to quantify, perceived value sits below economic value until you prove it.
Counting 'processes invoices 50% faster' and '200 staff hours saved' as separate benefits when they're the same benefit.

flashcards.front: Observed vs calculated vs assumed value
flashcards.back: Observed: measured from real customers. Calculated: derived from observed inputs. Assumed: a judgement. Your case is only as strong as its biggest assumed line.

flashcards.front: Lending: next best alternatives and differentiation for an SME advance?
flashcards.back: Alternatives: overdraft, term loan, credit card, other revenue-based funders, not borrowing. Plus: speed, flexible repayment, no fixed term. Minus: higher total cost.
A feature is what the product does; an outcome is what changes for the customer (hours, revenue, risk). Value and price should be anchored on outcomes.

flashcards.front: Two tests for a useful pricing segment
flashcards.back: 1) It differs in WTP, cost to serve, behaviour or value received. 2) You can identify it at the point of sale.
A rule that decides who qualifies for a price, stopping high-WTP customers from buying at the low price.
Product (versions), buyer (who you are), transaction (when/how/how much you buy), controlled availability (limited stock at a price).
Buying at a low-price segment and reselling or using it in a high-price one. Weak fences invite it.
Three tiers that let customers self-select by WTP. Each needs a target customer and a clear upgrade reason.
When shown three options, many people pick the middle. A premium tier makes the middle look reasonable.
Pure: only the bundle is sold. Mixed: bundle and individual items both available, usually with a bundle discount.

flashcards.front: When does bundling add the most value?
flashcards.back: When customers' WTPs for the items are negatively correlated - one values X more, another values Y more - so their bundle valuations are similar.

flashcards.front: A: X=8, Y=3. B: X=5, Y=6. Best separate revenue vs best bundle revenue?
flashcards.back: Separate: 16 (X at 5, Y at 3 or 6). Bundle at 11: 22.
A fixed fee plus a usage price. Captures value from light and heavy users. E.g. membership + per-class fee.
The unit you charge by (seats, transactions, % of volume). It should grow with the value the customer gets.
When a new or cheaper offer takes sales from your own higher-margin offers rather than winning new customers.

flashcards.front: Why avoid a deliberately unusable entry tier?
flashcards.back: Customers feel tricked, trust falls, and the tier generates support cost without revenue. Entry should be genuinely useful but limited.

flashcards.front: Feature that belongs in a tier vs one that's just expensive to serve?
flashcards.back: Tier features should map to value differences customers will pay for. A feature that's costly but not valued should be repriced or dropped, not used to justify a tier.

flashcards.front: Fairness test for a price difference?
flashcards.back: Could you explain it to the customer and a regulator? Differences tied to volume, timing or features pass; differences based on protected characteristics fail.

flashcards.front: Lending: what makes a good fence for risk-based pricing tiers?
flashcards.back: Data observable at application and hard to fake (trading history, card turnover, sector), explainable to the merchant, and not a proxy for protected characteristics.

flashcards.front: Why limit the number of options?
flashcards.back: Beyond 3-4, choice overload slows buyers and sales reps start improvising - which destroys the discipline the architecture was meant to create.
The specific moment or need that pushes a customer to the next tier (more users, more volume, a feature they hit). Design it in deliberately.

flashcards.front: Four market structures (least to most pricing power)
flashcards.back: Perfect competition, monopolistic competition, oligopoly, monopoly.
A few big players who watch and react. Every price move invites a response, so predict reactions before moving.

flashcards.front: When is a competitor's price informative?
flashcards.back: Only when the offer, customer, transaction terms and channel are comparable. Otherwise normalise first.
Adjusting for package size, features, service, contract length, payment terms, fees and discounts so you compare total value for total cost.
Each firm is tempted to cut price to win share; when both do, both end up worse off than if neither had.
Because rivals meet repeatedly, predictable responses to undercutting discourage it. Today's move shapes tomorrow's reaction.
An action that makes your future behaviour believable to rivals (e.g. capacity already built, a public guarantee), changing how they respond.
One firm sets price moves and others tend to follow. Lawful only when it arises without coordination.

flashcards.front: Why do price wars often destroy value?
flashcards.back: Firms react to visible prices without diagnosing why they're losing share. Margin is sacrificed, rivals match, and nobody gains share.

flashcards.front: Non-price causes of share loss to rule out
flashcards.back: Product gaps, stock-outs or capacity limits, service problems, weak sales coverage, losing a channel or partner.

flashcards.front: Price 100, cost 60. Competitor cuts 10%. If you match, what volume loss would make holding price equally good?
flashcards.back: 25%. Matching gives 30/unit x all units = 75% of 40/unit, so holding wins unless you lose more than 25%.
Targeted: respond only in the segments or accounts genuinely at risk. Broad: reprice everyone. Targeted usually costs far less margin.
Premium leader, parity player, disruptor, focused specialist. Your role should guide how you respond to competitor moves.
Never discuss or exchange future pricing or competitively sensitive information with competitors, directly or via third parties.
A supplier fixing the price resellers must charge. Usually prohibited; recommended prices are generally allowed.
A clause requiring a supplier not to offer a better price elsewhere. Can restrict competition and attracts regulatory scrutiny.

flashcards.front: Lending: competitor quotes 1.20 factor vs your 1.28. What do you check first?
flashcards.back: Holdback %, extra fees, early-settlement discount, advance size, speed to fund and eligibility. Only then compare total cost and expected duration.
An incumbent keeps prices low enough that entering the market looks unprofitable to newcomers.

flashcards.front: List vs invoice vs pocket price
flashcards.back: List: published. Invoice: after on-invoice discounts. Pocket: after all off-invoice deductions too (rebates, terms, freight, promotions).
The spread of pocket prices across similar customers buying similar products. A wide band usually signals inconsistent negotiation, not value differences.

flashcards.front: Five ways to slice a waterfall for leakage
flashcards.back: By customer, salesperson, product, channel and deduction type.
Earned: tied to a customer commitment (volume, term, prepayment). Habitual: given out of routine, with nothing in return.
The allowed discount range for a type of deal, usually split into green (rep approves), amber (manager) and red (deal desk/finance).
The minimum price below which no deal is approved, regardless of circumstances.
A central team that reviews and approves non-standard or out-of-corridor deals and keeps pricing consistent.
A recorded reason for approving an out-of-policy deal. Lets you spot patterns - repeated exceptions mean the policy needs revisiting.

flashcards.front: Why do revenue-based commissions undermine pricing?
flashcards.back: A discount costs the rep a little commission but the company much more contribution, so reps rationally trade margin for a faster close.

flashcards.front: Margin 40%. A 10% discount needs how much extra volume to break even?

flashcards.back: Every concession is exchanged for a customer commitment: volume, term, prepayment, faster decision, reference, scope.

flashcards.front: Non-price variables to trade in a negotiation
flashcards.back: Contract length, volume commitment, payment terms, prepayment, implementation timing, service level, scope, auto-renewal, being a reference customer.
Pocket (or net) price as a % of list price. Tracks how much of the intended price you actually keep.

flashcards.front: Comparable deals average 5% more discount than needed on 20m revenue. Profit at stake?
flashcards.back: About 1m - and it drops almost entirely to profit, because no costs change.

flashcards.front: What should a discount policy tell a rep?
flashcards.back: What they can approve themselves, what needs approval and from whom, what to ask for in return, and the floor - at the moment of quoting.

flashcards.front: Lending: common sources of price leakage
flashcards.back: Commission overrides, fees waived at renewal, unpriced early-settlement discounts, advances rounded up beyond approval.

flashcards.front: Why reconcile the waterfall to net revenue?
flashcards.back: If it doesn't tie to finance's numbers, nobody will trust the leakage findings - and you might be missing deductions booked elsewhere.

flashcards.front: Better fix for over-discounting: tighter approvals or changed incentives?
flashcards.back: Usually incentives. Approvals catch outliers, but paying on margin or price realisation changes behaviour on every deal.

flashcards.front: Four conditions where revenue management pays off
flashcards.back: Constrained capacity, perishable inventory, variable demand, and customers booking at different times (with different WTP).
Dynamic: price changes with market conditions; everyone sees the same price at a given moment. Personalised: price changes with information about the individual.

flashcards.front: Why is personalised pricing riskier than dynamic pricing?
flashcards.back: Two people see different prices at the same moment based on who they are. It raises fairness, transparency and legal concerns and damages trust if discovered.
A price level for the same capacity, with its own fences and availability. Revenue management opens and closes classes as demand unfolds.
Keep protecting capacity for the high fare while P(high-fare demand > protected units) x high fare >= low fare.

flashcards.front: Full fare 300, discount 100. Protect a seat while P(full-fare demand exceeds it) is at least what?

flashcards.back: Choosing when and how deeply to discount seasonal or perishable stock to balance margin against sell-through and leftover risk.
Units sold as a % of units available. The key leading indicator for markdown decisions.

flashcards.front: When do revenue-maximising and profit-maximising prices differ?
flashcards.back: Whenever variable costs matter. Extra units at a lower price add revenue but may add little or negative contribution.

flashcards.front: Price 8 sells 1,500; price 12 sells 900. Variable cost 5. Which price maximises contribution?
flashcards.back: 12. Contribution 6,300 vs 4,500, even though revenue is lower (10,800 vs 12,000).

flashcards.front: Why can a mathematically optimal price be commercially weak?
flashcards.back: Forecast error, competitor reactions, cancellations and operational limits. A price that's robust across scenarios often beats one optimal only in the base case.
Selling more than capacity because some customers cancel or don't show. Balances empty-seat cost against the cost of denying service.
Floor price or minimum margin, ceiling, max % change per period, freeze in emergencies, channel consistency, no use of sensitive data.
Customer fairness, transparency, price volatility, brand, and operational feasibility.

flashcards.front: Lending: how is funding capacity like an airline seat?
flashcards.back: When capital is limited, each advance uses up capacity with an opportunity cost. Allocate it by risk-adjusted return per pound, not by volume.

flashcards.front: Why test RM decisions under low, expected and high demand?
flashcards.back: The base forecast will be wrong. Scenarios show how much you lose if it is, and whether a different rule is more robust.

flashcards.front: Which demand signals matter for dynamic pricing?
flashcards.back: Those that arrive early enough to act on: bookings pace, search or quote volume, competitor moves, inventory levels, events.

flashcards.front: Ten fields in a useful pricing dataset
flashcards.back: Realised price, units, product, customer, time, channel, promotions, availability, cost, and relevant market variables.
An unmeasured factor affects both price and volume, so the price coefficient absorbs its effect.
Demand influences price (prices set high when demand is strong), so price-volume correlation isn't purely price causing volume.

flashcards.front: Why does randomisation give a causal estimate?
flashcards.back: Random assignment makes groups alike on average in everything except price, so outcome differences are caused by price.
What gets randomised: customer, account, store, region or time period. Choose one that limits contamination and suits operations.
Control units are exposed to the treatment, or vice versa - e.g. customers seeing both prices, or reps working both groups.
Change price in some markets and compare with similar unchanged markets chosen to match on size, trend and mix.
(Treated after - treated before) - (control after - control before). Removes trends shared by both groups.
The identifying assumption of DiD: without the change, treated and control groups would have moved in parallel. Check pre-period trends.
A weighted blend of untreated units built to track the treated unit before the change; its post-change path is the counterfactual.
Introduce the change in waves; units not yet switched act as controls for those already switched.
The smallest effect the test is designed to reliably detect. Smaller MDE needs a much bigger sample.

flashcards.front: Sample size rule of thumb (80% power, 5% significance)
flashcards.back: n per group = 16 x p(1-p) / d^2, where p is the baseline rate and d the effect to detect.

flashcards.front: Baseline conversion 20%, want to detect 2 points. Sample per group?
Why make incremental contribution the primary outcome?
flashcards.back: Higher prices usually lower conversion but raise margin. Conversion or revenue alone can reject a profitable price - or accept an unprofitable one.
A metric that must not deteriorate beyond a set limit (complaints, churn, loss rate), triggering a stop regardless of the primary result.
It stops people moving the goalposts after seeing results. Launch, revise and reject thresholds are fixed in advance.

flashcards.front: Lending: leading indicators for a price test (losses take months)
flashcards.back: Take-up rate, mix of risk grades accepted, early repayment velocity, early arrears or missed-collection signals.

flashcards.front: Six things every pricing launch needs
flashcards.back: Effective date, affected customers, transition rules, system changes, owners, escalation paths.
Letting existing customers keep the old price for a period or until renewal. Protects retention; delays the revenue benefit.
How customers move to the new price: notice periods, renewal timing, grandfathering, honouring in-flight quotes.

flashcards.front: Good customer communication about a price change
flashcards.back: What changes, when, and why - linked to value delivered, with fair notice and no unsupported claims.
A short, consistent script for reps to explain the change and its value in their own words.

flashcards.front: Five parts of sales enablement for a price change
flashcards.back: Talk tracks, objection handling, approval rules, worked examples, and practice on realistic deals.
Acknowledge, ask what they're comparing against, reframe on outcomes and value, and only trade price for a commitment.
Responsible (does it), Accountable (owns the decision - exactly one), Consulted (gives input), Informed (kept updated).

flashcards.front: Five pricing decisions that need clear decision rights
flashcards.back: List prices, discounts, promotions, exceptions, and post-launch corrections.

flashcards.front: What do repeated exceptions tell you?
flashcards.back: The policy doesn't match reality. Either the corridor is wrong or enablement is failing - review and change one of them.

flashcards.front: Six things a post-launch scorecard tracks separately
flashcards.back: Adoption, realised price, volume response, mix, customer retention, financial return.
Implementation failure: the price never really reached customers (systems, discounting). Flawed hypothesis: it did, and customers reacted worse than predicted.

flashcards.front: Why must every launch task have an owner, date and dependency?
flashcards.back: Without them, tasks slip silently and nobody knows which delay blocks the go-live.
Scheduled reviews (e.g. weeks 2, 6, 12) with pre-agreed triggers to keep, adjust or roll back the change.

flashcards.front: Lending: customer cohorts for a pricing change
flashcards.back: New merchants, renewing merchants, and partner channels presenting offers - each may need different timing, messaging and systems.

flashcards.front: Why do under-prepared reps undo a price rise?
flashcards.back: Without confidence or answers to objections, they fall back on discounting - which quietly cancels the increase.

flashcards.front: Six elements of a decision-ready recommendation
flashcards.back: The decision, financial effect, customer logic, evidence, operational plan, and material risks.

flashcards.front: What goes on the first slide?
flashcards.back: The decision requested: proposed price, scope, effective date, approval needed - plus the headline financial effect.
Lead with the answer, then the supporting arguments, then the detail. Lets busy readers decide after one page.

flashcards.front: Why show base, downside and upside?
flashcards.back: A single number hides uncertainty. Ranges with stated assumptions show the risk and earn more trust than false precision.
Sensitivity chart ranking assumptions by how much they move the result when flexed. Shows what to test first.

flashcards.front: Fact vs estimate vs assumption vs choice
flashcards.back: Fact: observed. Estimate: derived from data, with uncertainty. Assumption: judgement without strong data. Choice: a management value call.
A chart walking from baseline to new profit through separate effects: price, volume, mix, cost. Must reconcile to the model.

flashcards.front: Price and volume effects in a bridge
flashcards.back: Price effect = price change x new volume. Volume effect = volume change x old unit contribution. They sum to the total change.

flashcards.front: Price 100 to 105, volume 10,000 to 9,300, cost 60. Price effect and volume effect?

flashcards.back: Pre-agreed results at set review dates: stop if guardrails break, adjust if a segment underperforms, expand if results beat the base case.
Every price change redistributes value. Name the customers, channels and teams most exposed, so leadership approves the risk knowingly.
Have someone attack your elasticity, cost, value and implementation assumptions before leadership does - then revise.
Decision, business context, baseline economics, demand evidence, customer value, price design, financial return, commercial plan, measurement, risks.
Pricing economics, financial return, customer and market evidence, commercial design, implementation and measurement.
At least 70 of 100 overall AND at least 12 in every area. A weak area is a material weakness even with a high total.

flashcards.front: Which assumption should you test first?
flashcards.back: The one that contributes most to the financial return and is least certain - usually found with a sensitivity analysis.

flashcards.front: First data-quality check before any price realisation analysis?
flashcards.back: Reconcile transaction totals to the finance source.

flashcards.front: What to do with returns, credits, zero prices and negative quantities
flashcards.back: Flag them - don't silently delete them. They can be real leakage or real behaviour.

flashcards.front: Four things to standardise before comparing transactions
flashcards.back: Currency, tax treatment, units of measure, and time periods.

flashcards.front: Can you mix list, invoice and pocket price in one analysis?
flashcards.back: No. Pick one definition and use it consistently, or results won't reconcile.
Incremental profit / implementation cost, over a defined period. State whether profit is gross, contribution or operating.
New contribution - old contribution - implementation cost.
Fixed cost / unit contribution. Fixed 250k, unit contribution 40: 6,250 units.

flashcards.front: Five columns of the research log
flashcards.back: Source, main claim, evidence, limitations, decision impact. The point is linking research to a decision, not collecting links.

quiz.question: Price 80, cost 60. What is the markup?
quiz.explanation: Markup = (80 - 60) / 60 = 33.3%. The margin would be 25%.

quiz.question: Contribution margin 40%. You raise price 5%. Which volume change makes total contribution fall?
quiz.explanation: Break-even volume loss is 0.05 / 0.45 = 11.1%. Only the 12% loss exceeds it.

quiz.question: You have spare capacity and are offered a one-off discounted order. Which cost is relevant?
quiz.explanation: Only costs that change because you accept the order are relevant. The others are incurred either way.

quiz.question: Unit contribution falls from 40 to 35. How many units keep contribution at the 10,000-unit level?
quiz.explanation: Required volume = 10,000 x 40 / 35 = 11,429, a 14.3% increase.

quiz.question: Two MCAs both have a 1.30 factor rate. A repays in 6 months, B in 12. Ignoring losses, which is true?
options: A has the higher annualised return
B has the higher annualised return
You can't compare them without the advance size
quiz.explanation: The same fee earned over half the time means a much higher annualised return. The factor rate alone doesn't tell you the yield.

quiz.question: Rebates are being paid to customers who never hit the volume target. What kind of fix does this need?
options: A pricing action: lower list prices
A process action: enforce rebate eligibility
A cost action: cut variable cost
quiz.explanation: The policy is fine; execution is leaking. That's a process fix.

quiz.question: Price 100, variable cost 60, 10,000 units. Price +5%, volume -7%. New total contribution, in thousands?
List 100. On-invoice discount 8, rebate 3, payment terms cost 1.50, freight 2, co-op marketing 1.50. Pocket price?
Target margin 35% on a cost of 65. What price?
quiz.explanation: Price = cost / (1 - margin) = 65 / 0.65 = 100.

quiz.question: Elasticity is -0.5. You raise price 10%. What happens to revenue?
quiz.explanation: Volume falls about 5%. Revenue = 1.10 x 0.95 = 1.045, up about 4.5%.

quiz.question: Cross-price elasticity between A and B is +0.6. A and B are:
quiz.explanation: When B's price rises, demand for A rises, so customers treat them as alternatives.

quiz.question: A retailer raised prices in December and sales rose. The best explanation is:
options: Seasonal demand shifted the curve, confounding the price effect
Elasticity is positive for this product
quiz.explanation: Christmas demand moved the whole curve. You can't read elasticity from this without controlling for season.

quiz.question: Elasticity is -3. By the Lerner rule, the profit-maximising margin is about:
You raise factor rates 5% and offer take-up barely changes. What should you check before calling it a success?
options: Nothing, take-up is the key metric
Whether the risk mix and loss rates of accepted merchants changed
quiz.explanation: In lending, price can change who accepts. Riskier merchants may be less price-sensitive, so losses can rise even when volume holds.

quiz.question: Prices are typically raised when demand is strong. A naive regression of volume on price will most likely:
options: Understate how elastic demand is (bias towards zero)
quiz.explanation: High prices coincide with high demand, so the estimated slope is pulled towards zero or even positive.

quiz.question: Price 20 to 22, quantity 500 to 460. Arc elasticity (to 2 decimals)?
Contribution margin 30%. Price +10%. What is the break-even elasticity?
quiz.explanation: Break-even volume loss = 0.10 / 0.40 = 25%. 25% / 10% = elasticity of -2.5.

quiz.question: Which method best decides which features go into a premium tier?
quiz.explanation: Conjoint estimates the value of each feature via trade-offs, which is exactly the package design question.

quiz.question: The main limitation of Van Westendorp is that it:
options: Doesn't measure how many people would buy
quiz.explanation: It gives an acceptable range but no purchase likelihood, so you can't use it to estimate revenue.

quiz.question: A survey says 60% would pay 20. At launch 15% buy. The most likely cause is:
quiz.explanation: With no money at stake, respondents overstate WTP.

quiz.question: EVC is 13k and the competitor charges 10k. If you price at 13k:
options: You capture maximum profit with no downside
The customer is roughly indifferent and has little reason to switch
You are below the reference value
quiz.explanation: At EVC the customer gains nothing by switching. Price between 10k and 13k to share value.

quiz.question: Which is negative differentiation value?
options: Your implementation takes 3 months vs the competitor's 1 week
quiz.explanation: A longer implementation is a cost the customer bears with you but not the alternative.

quiz.question: Competitor charges 50/month. Your product saves an extra 20/month but needs 5/month more in setup costs. EVC per month?
Which is the weakest price fence?
options: Self-declared 'small business' status with no check
quiz.explanation: Self-declared status is easy to misrepresent, so high-WTP customers can claim it.

quiz.question: A gym charges a monthly membership plus a fee per class. This is:
quiz.explanation: Fixed fee plus a usage price is a two-part tariff.

quiz.question: A new cheaper tier mostly attracts existing premium customers who downgrade. This is:
quiz.explanation: The new offer takes sales from your own higher-margin offer instead of winning new customers.

quiz.question: Which is NOT usable as a pricing segment at the point of sale?
options: The customer's true maximum willingness to pay
quiz.explanation: True WTP is unobservable. You need observable proxies to fence on.

quiz.question: For a payments platform, the value metric most aligned with customer value is usually:
options: A percentage of transaction value processed
quiz.explanation: Processed value grows with the benefit the merchant gets from the platform.

quiz.question: A values X at 10 and Y at 2. B values X at 6 and Y at 7. What is the maximum revenue from selling a pure bundle to both?
quiz.explanation: A values the bundle at 12, B at 13. Price at 12 so both buy: 24. Best separate pricing earns only 19.

quiz.question: A competitor's list price is 10% lower but excludes onboarding and support. What should you do first?
quiz.explanation: Without normalising, you can't tell whether they're actually cheaper.

quiz.question: Which activity is a clear competition-law risk?
options: Checking a rival's public website prices
Discussing next quarter's rates with a rival at a conference
Buying a competitor's product to test it
quiz.explanation: Sharing future pricing intentions with competitors can amount to collusion.

quiz.question: Share fell in one region, where you had repeated stock-outs. The most likely cause is:
options: An availability problem, not a price problem
quiz.explanation: Customers can't buy what isn't there. Cutting price wouldn't fix it.

quiz.question: Two firms both cut prices hoping to win share, and both end up less profitable. This illustrates:
quiz.explanation: Individually rational moves produce a collectively worse outcome.

quiz.question: A competitor cut prices, but only small, price-sensitive accounts are switching. The best response is usually:
options: A targeted response for the at-risk segment
quiz.explanation: A targeted response protects the vulnerable segment without giving margin away on accounts that weren't leaving.

quiz.question: Price 50, variable cost 35, 20,000 units. A competitor cuts 10%. If you hold price, what % volume loss would make matching equally good? (1 decimal)
quiz.explanation: Matching: 20,000 x 10 = 200,000. Holding: units x 15. Break-even units = 13,333, a 33.3% loss.

quiz.question: Corridor: 0-10% green, 10-15% amber, above 15% deal desk. A rep wants 18%. What happens?
options: It goes to the deal desk with an exception code
quiz.explanation: Above 15% is outside the amber band, so it needs deal desk approval and a recorded reason.

quiz.question: Reps are paid 5% of revenue and discount heavily near quarter-end. The most effective structural fix is:
options: Paying commission on margin or price realisation
quiz.explanation: Aligning pay with contribution changes the incentive on every deal.

quiz.question: Which is a good give-get trade?
options: 5% off for a 24-month term and annual upfront payment
5% off because a competitor might be cheaper
quiz.explanation: The concession buys commitments that are worth something to the business.

quiz.question: Similar customers buying similar volumes have pocket prices ranging from 78 to 91. This suggests:
options: Inconsistent negotiation and an opportunity to tighten policy
quiz.explanation: If the customers are comparable, the spread reflects negotiation outcomes, not value.

quiz.question: Margin 30%. A rep gives a 10% discount. What % volume increase is needed to keep contribution flat?
Advance 50,000 at factor 1.30. Commission 8% of advance, expected loss 5% of repayable, cost of funds 1,875, servicing 500. Pocket fee?
Which business is the best fit for classic revenue management?
options: A bakery selling bread by weight
quiz.explanation: Fixed, perishable rooms; variable demand; guests booking at different times with different WTP.

quiz.question: Showing a higher price to a user because their device suggests they're wealthy is:
quiz.explanation: The price changes based on information about the individual, not market conditions.

quiz.question: Price 8 sells 1,500; price 12 sells 900; variable cost 5. Which statement is true?
quiz.explanation: Revenue: 12,000 vs 10,800. Contribution: 4,500 vs 6,300.

quiz.question: Full fare 200, discount 80. Under Littlewood's rule, accept a discount booking (rather than protect the seat) when the probability that full-fare demand exceeds the protected seats is:
quiz.explanation: Protect while P x 200 >= 80, i.e. P >= 0.4. Below that, the certain 80 is worth more.

quiz.question: Which is a pricing guardrail?
options: A cap of 10% on daily price changes
Using customer browsing history to set prices
quiz.explanation: A rate limit stops prices swinging in ways that damage trust and brand.

quiz.question: 100 units left. Hold at 50: sell 60, leftovers worth 0. Mark down to 35: sell 95. How much more revenue does the markdown earn?
The identifying assumption of difference-in-differences is:
options: Parallel trends between treated and control without the change
quiz.explanation: DiD assumes the control group shows what would have happened to the treated group.

quiz.question: Which is contamination?
options: Test and control regions differ in size
Reps sell to customers in both test and control territories
quiz.explanation: Reps can carry pricing or behaviour across groups, blurring the comparison.

quiz.question: The best primary metric for a price test is usually:
quiz.explanation: It captures both the margin gain and the volume loss.

quiz.question: Prices were raised first where demand was strongest. A regression of volume on price will likely:
options: Be unbiased if there are enough rows
quiz.explanation: Reverse causality pushes the estimate towards zero.

quiz.question: Treatment conversion 20% to 18%. Control 21% to 20%. DiD effect in percentage points?
Baseline conversion 10%, effect to detect 2 points, 80% power. Rough sample per group?
Control: 1,000 visitors, 20% convert, contribution 40 each. Test: 1,000 visitors, 17% convert, contribution 50 each. Test minus control contribution?
List price changed correctly in all systems, but realised price barely moved. The most likely cause is:
quiz.explanation: If adoption is fine but realisation isn't, discounting is eating the change.

quiz.question: In a RACI matrix, how many people should be Accountable for one decision?
quiz.explanation: One accountable owner avoids ambiguity about who decides.

quiz.question: Grandfathering existing customers mainly trades:
options: Higher short-term revenue for lower retention
Slower revenue benefit for better retention and goodwill
quiz.explanation: You give up some early revenue to reduce churn risk among existing customers.

quiz.question: 40% of deals use the 'competitive' exception code. What should governance do?
options: Review the corridor or enablement, since the exception has become the norm
quiz.explanation: Repeated exceptions signal that policy and reality have diverged.

quiz.question: Which customer message is best?
options: 'Costs went up so prices go up.'
'From 1 March the fee rises 4%, funding same-day payouts.'
'We're still the cheapest in the market.' (unverified)
quiz.explanation: Clear timing, honest, and linked to value - without unsupported claims.

quiz.question: What should appear on the first page or slide?
quiz.explanation: Lead with the ask so the reader knows what they're deciding.

quiz.question: 'Competitors won't respond for six months' is best labelled as:
quiz.explanation: It's a judgement without strong data - exactly what a challenge session should test.

quiz.question: A capstone scores 78 overall, with 10 in implementation and measurement. Does it pass?
options: No, every area needs at least 12
Yes, if the financial return is strong
quiz.explanation: The standard requires 70 overall AND 12 in every area.

quiz.question: A tornado chart shows elasticity moves the result far more than any other input. You should:
options: Ignore it; it's just a chart
Prioritise testing or refining the elasticity estimate
quiz.explanation: Spend evidence-gathering effort on the assumption that matters most.

quiz.question: Price 100 to 105, volume 10,000 to 9,300, variable cost 60. Price effect in the profit bridge?
Same case. Volume effect in the profit bridge?
quiz.explanation: -700 units x 40 old unit contribution = -28,000.

formulas.name: Gross margin percent
formulas.interpretation: Measures gross profit as a share of sales.

formulas.name: Markup percent
formulas.interpretation: Measures the increase over cost and is not interchangeable with margin.

formulas.name: Unit contribution
formulas.formula: Net price - Variable cost per unit
formulas.interpretation: Measures the amount available to cover fixed cost and profit.

formulas.name: Break even volume
formulas.interpretation: Calculates units required to cover fixed costs.

formulas.name: Price elasticity
formulas.formula: % change in quantity / % change in price
formulas.interpretation: Measures demand response. It is normally negative for ordinary goods.

formulas.name: Required new volume
formulas.formula: Old volume x Old unit contribution / New unit contribution
formulas.interpretation: Keeps total contribution unchanged when variable cost per unit is stable.

formulas.name: Incremental profit
formulas.formula: New contribution - Old contribution - Implementation cost
formulas.interpretation: Captures the change attributable to the initiative.

formulas.name: Pricing initiative ROI
formulas.interpretation: Use a defined time period and state whether profit is gross, contribution, or operating.

formulas.name: Margin to markup
formulas.interpretation: Converts a margin into the equivalent markup on cost.

formulas.name: Markup to margin
formulas.interpretation: Converts a markup on cost into the equivalent margin on price.

formulas.name: Break-even volume change
formulas.interpretation: Volume change that keeps contribution flat after a price change; dP and CM% as fractions of the old price.

formulas.name: Arc (midpoint) elasticity
formulas.formula: [(Q2 - Q1) / avg Q] / [(P2 - P1) / avg P]
formulas.interpretation: Elasticity between two observed points, same in either direction.

formulas.name: Lerner rule
formulas.interpretation: Profit-maximising margin given a constant elasticity.

formulas.name: Economic value to the customer
formulas.formula: Reference value + Positive differentiation - Negative differentiation
formulas.interpretation: The most an informed customer should pay; price below it to share value.

formulas.name: Littlewood's rule
formulas.formula: Protect while P(high demand > protected) x High fare >= Low fare
formulas.interpretation: How much capacity to hold back for higher-paying, later demand.

formulas.name: Difference-in-differences
formulas.formula: (Treated after - Treated before) - (Control after - Control before)
formulas.interpretation: Effect of a change, net of trends shared with the control group.

formulas.name: Sample size rule of thumb
formulas.formula: n per group = 16 x p(1 - p) / d^2
formulas.interpretation: Approximate sample for 80% power at 5% significance when comparing two rates.

formulas.name: Profit bridge: price and volume effects
formulas.formula: Price effect = dP x New volume. Volume effect = dVolume x Old unit contribution.
formulas.interpretation: Splits a contribution change into its price and volume drivers.

capstone_structure.content: State the proposed price, scope, effective date, and approval requested.
Explain the customer, product, market, and problem being solved.
Show price realization, revenue, contribution, costs, and current leakage.
Present elasticity, research, comparable evidence, and limitations.
Explain the next best alternative, differentiation value, and willingness to pay evidence.
Show segments, packages, fences, metrics, and transaction rules.
Present base, downside, and upside cases with break even conditions and initiative ROI.
Cover sales enablement, communications, systems, contracts, owners, and timeline.
Define test design, KPIs, guardrails, review cadence, and decision rules.
Name the largest assumptions and the actions that reduce or monitor each risk.

areas.evidence: Correct unit economics, relevant costs, price volume tradeoff, and break even analysis.
Clear profit bridge, scenarios, ROI, assumptions, and reconciliation.
Credible value, willingness to pay, elasticity, segmentation, and competitive evidence.
Operable price architecture, discount rules, customer treatment, and sales logic.
Owners, timeline, systems, governance, KPIs, risks, and decision rules.

scoring_guide.passing_standard: Aim for at least 70 points overall and at least 12 points in every area. A low score in one area signals a material weakness even when the total score is high. Revise the capstone until the financial case, customer evidence, commercial design, and implementation plan are mutually consistent.

minimum_dataset.fields: SKU, family, package, attributes, lifecycle stage
Anonymous identifier, segment, geography, channel, new or existing status
List price, invoice price, discounts, rebates, freight, service deductions, pocket price
Variable cost, cost to serve, contribution, payment terms
Promotion, availability, competitor price, season, relevant demand drivers
Conversion, units, revenue, retention, returns or cancellations when relevant

data_quality_checks: Reconcile transaction totals to the finance source before calculating price realization or profit.
Separate list price, invoice price, and pocket price. Do not mix them within one analysis.
Flag returns, cancellations, free units, credits, zero prices, and negative quantities instead of silently deleting them.
Standardize currency, tax treatment, units of measure, and time periods before comparing transactions.
Control for promotions, stockouts, product changes, and major market events when estimating demand response.
Protect customer confidentiality and use the minimum personal data required for the decision.
